title: Why 11% of PINs are 1234, and how to pick a safe one
description:
A four-digit PIN has 10,000 possible codes, so a thief with 3 tries before the card locks should get in only 3 times in 10,000. But people don't pick at random: in 3.4 million leaked four-digit codes, almost 11% were 1234, and the 20 most common codes covered 27%. Dates are almost as bad: a month and day leaves only 366 codes, and a year starting with 19 leaves 100, so 3 tries open 3 in 100, a hundred times worse than random. Let random numbers pick all four digits.

Numbers checked in code (code counts and a simulation of 2 million guesses); PIN frequencies from Nick Berry's DataGenetics PIN analysis (2012), as reported by HuffPost UK.

The math behind real problems, twice a day. Subscribe and the next one finds you.

facts_checked: 3.4 million four-digit codes from leaked password tables; almost 11% are 1234 (DataGenetics 10.713%); top 20 codes cover 26.83% (https://huffingtonpost.co.uk/entry/worst-pin-numbers_n_3696560, citing http://www.datagenetics.com/blog/september32012/, which returned 503 today)
1234, 1111, 0000 are the three most common in the published top 10 (HuffPost UK, same article)
10,000 possible codes; 3 random tries open 3 in 10,000 (verify.py, simulated 2,000,000 tries: 3.05)
Month-and-day codes: 366; codes starting with 19: 100; 3 tries open 3 in 100, 100x worse than random (verify.py, simulated: 2.99)
Bank cards lock after a few wrong PIN tries (3 is the usual limit); stated as the scenario, not a universal rule

beats.say: Nearly 11% of PINs are one two three four.
Ten thousand codes sounds safe. A thief gets 3 tries, then the card locks.
If you'd picked at random, those 3 tries open 3 cards in 10,000.
But people don't. In 3.4 million leaked codes, the top 20 covered 27%.
So step one: no patterns. Not one two three four, not four ones, not four zeros.
Step two is the one people miss. Your birthday.
A month and day leaves just 366 codes. A year starting with 19 leaves 100.
And your wallet holds your ID. Then 3 tries open 3 cards in 100: 100 times worse than random.
Step three: let random numbers pick all four digits, and keep them.
Ten thousand codes only protect you if yours could be any of them.
Subscribe if you thought 10,000 was safe.
